Burbot early life stages are characterized by remarkably small size. At the moment of egg hatching, which occurs under cold incubation temperatures, the prolarvae emerge at a total length of just 0.42 cm . The tiny yolk-sac larvae, still lecithotrophic and largely immobile, measure approximately 0.46 cm [Lb = approximately 0.46 cm] in total length at birth, representing the stage when they become free from the chorion and begin a brief period of endogenous nutrition. The wet weight at this initial birth event is only 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams], reflecting the small egg diameter of roughly one millimeter from which they originate. These minute dimensions place the burbot among the smallest-born gadiform larvae, a trait linked to the production of numerous pelagic eggs in cold, unproductive environments. The time since hatch at birth is relatively brief, lasting only about 8 days  when water temperatures hover near 10 °C [T = 10 °C], after which the larvae must transition to exogenous feeding before their yolk reserves are fully exhausted, a critical period known as the point of no return.

The incubation period for burbot eggs is strongly dependent on thermal conditions. At a sustained water temperature of 3 °C [T = 3 °C], embryos require approximately 30 days  to complete development and undergo eclosion. This extended incubation period is typical for cold-water adapted teleosts and allows for gradual differentiation of the blastula-stage embryo into a functional yolk-sac larva. Following hatching, the prolarval stage is dominated by the progressive absorption of yolk nutrients, during which the larvae remain largely quiescent near the bottom. Interestingly, some reports indicate that at slightly warmer temperatures, such as 4 °C, the incubation period can shorten to around 24 days, highlighting the sensitivity of embryonic metabolic rates to even small thermal shifts. The hatching event itself involves chorionase secretion and chorion rupture, and the newly emerged alevins are notably transparent, with a prominent yolk sac that sustains them through the first days of life before the onset of active feeding.

As burbot grow, they undergo a steady increase in body size, eventually reaching an ultimate total length that can be quite impressive. The maximum recorded total length for this species is 152 cm [Li = 152 cm], a size that places it among the larger members of the Lotidae family. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight attained by a fully grown adult is approximately 34,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 34,000 grams], though such massive individuals are rarely encountered and typically represent the upper tail of the size distribution in pristine northern waters. The growth trajectory from the small larval stages to these enormous adults involves a prolonged juvenile phase. Under typical thermal regimes, juvenile burbot feed actively on benthic invertebrates and later on fish, accumulating the necessary biomass to fuel their long lifespan. The overall lifespan of the species is considerable, with the oldest documented individuals reaching an age of roughly 20 years [am = roughly 20 years] when maintained at a water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], although mortality from predation and senescence likely truncates this value in wild populations.

Reproductive maturation in burbot is reached after several years of growth. The total length at puberty, marking the onset of gonad maturation and vitellogenesis, is approximately 40 cm [Lp = approximately 40 cm]. At this size, individuals attain a wet weight at puberty of roughly 320 grams [Wwp = roughly 320 grams], a mass that is sufficient to support the energetic demands of gamete production. The time since hatch at puberty for burbot is about 4 years [tp = about 4 years] when they are reared at a water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], a duration that reflects the relatively slow life history pace typical of a large, cold-water predator. Once mature, the species exhibits a seasonal spawning migration into shallower waters during the winter months. Fecundity is high, with females producing between 1,000,000 and 1,500,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = between 1,000,000 and 1,500,000 eggs per spawning event], and they typically spawn only once per year [F_R_i = spawn only once per year], demonstrating a reproductive strategy that emphasizes high fecundity over repeated breeding bouts within a single season.

Burbot display notable physiological adaptations to their cold-water environment. Life at low temperatures imposes constraints on metabolic processes, and the species has evolved compensatory mechanisms to sustain activity. Field studies indicate that the resting metabolic rate of a 1,000-gram burbot is approximately 12.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour at 5 °C, though this value increases markedly with temperature. The species is primarily nocturnal and relies on a lateral line system to detect prey in the turbid, deep lakes and large rivers it inhabits across its Holarctic distribution. The maximum recorded longevity of 20 years [am = 20 years] at 13 °C [T = 13 °C] is exceptional among freshwater gadids and likely reflects both the low metabolic demands of its thermal niche and the low predation pressure on large adults. While the early life stages are highly vulnerable to environmental variability, the robust physiological design of the adult burbot enables it to persist across a broad latitudinal range, from the Arctic Circle to the temperate zone, making it a species of considerable interest for studies of life history evolution in extreme environments.
